sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Single Arm Dumbbell Tricep Extension is a unilateral isolation exercise targeting the triceps.

With one dumbbell held overhead, the lifter lowers it behind the head and presses it back up, working one arm at a time.

Training one arm at a time corrects strength imbalances and increases the demand on core stability.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Targets all three heads of the triceps with strong long-head emphasis
- Trains each arm independently to fix imbalances
- Improves shoulder mobility through the overhead position
- Reinforces core bracing and anti-lateral flexion
- Easy to load progressively with a single dumbbell
- Effective accessory for pressing strength
- Allows the free hand to support the working arm if needed

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Triceps Brachii

Secondary: Anconeus, Core, Anterior Deltoids, Obliques

sections.heading: Set Up
sections.content:
1. Choose a dumbbell that allows good form for the desired reps.
2. Stand with your feet hip-width apart.
3. Hold the dumbbell in one hand with a neutral grip.

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Raise the dumbbell over your head until your arm is fully extended.
2. Brace your core and slightly bend your knees.
3. Place your other hand on your waist for balance or use it to support the arm that's lifting.

sections.heading: Lower
sections.content:
1. Keep your upper arm close to your head and your elbow pointing upward.
2. Slowly lower the dumbbell behind your head by bending your elbow.
3. Continue until your forearm is at least parallel to the floor.

sections.heading: Press and Repeat
sections.content:
1. Contract your tricep to extend your elbow and raise the dumbbell back to the starting position.
2. Keep the upper arm stationary throughout the press.
3. Complete all reps on one side before switching arms.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Letting the elbow flare out wide
- Moving the upper arm instead of just the forearm
- Arching the lower back to lift the weight
- Going too heavy and losing control overhead
- Cutting the range of motion short
- Tilting the torso to one side
- Holding the breath through the rep

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Single dumbbell of appropriate weight
- Optional: Bench for a seated variation
- Athletic shoes for stable footing
- Optional: Mirror to monitor form

sections.heading: Dumbbell Adjustments
sections.content:
1. Select a dumbbell light enough to fully extend overhead with control.
2. Use a neutral grip with the palm facing inward.
3. Confirm the dumbbell is balanced before lifting overhead.
4. Adjust load progressively as strength improves.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Stance: Feet hip-width apart, knees soft.
2. Torso: Tall posture, ribs stacked over hips, core braced.
3. Working Arm: Upper arm close to the head, elbow pointing up.
4. Free Hand: On waist for balance or supporting the working arm.
5. Head: Neutral, eyes forward.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Tricep Dumbbell Extension: Two-handed overhead version
- Tricep Skull Crusher: Lying triceps extension
- Tricep Pushdown: Cable triceps isolation
- Cable Overhead Tricep Extension: Cable version of this movement
- Close Grip Bench Press: Compound triceps press
- Tricep Dips On Bench: Bodyweight triceps work

sections.heading: Single Arm Dumbbell Tricep Extension Variations
sections.content:
Standing Single Arm Overhead Extension: Described here
Seated Single Arm Overhead Extension: Performed seated for stability
Kneeling Single Arm Overhead Extension: Performed kneeling for added core demand
Supported Single Arm Overhead Extension: Bracing the working arm with the free hand
Cable Single Arm Overhead Extension: Cable version using a single handle
Incline Single Arm Overhead Extension: Performed on an incline bench

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Shoulder Mobility Issues: Use a lighter weight and reduce range overhead
Elbow Pain: Reduce load and avoid locking out aggressively
Wrist Pain: Use a neutral grip and wrist wraps if needed
Low Back Pain: Perform seated with back support
Balance Issues: Sit on a bench with back support
Beginners: Start light and use the free hand to support the working arm
